{{Short description|Measure of the degree to which a geometric shape is compact}}
{{distinguish|text=the topological notion of [[compact space]]}}
'''Compactness measure''' is a numerical quantity representing the degree to which a [[shape]] is [[:wikt:compact|compact]]. The circle and the sphere are the most compact planar and solid shapes, respectively.

==Properties==
Various compactness measures are used.  However, these measures have the following in common:

*They are applicable to all geometric shapes.
*They are independent of scale and orientation.
*They are [[dimensionless number]]s.
*They are not overly dependent on one or two extreme [[point (geometry)|points]] in the shape.
*They agree with intuitive notions of what makes a shape compact.

==Examples==
A common compactness measure is the [[isoperimetric quotient]], the ratio of the area of the shape to the area of a [[circle]] (the most compact shape) having the same perimeter.  In the [[plane (geometry)|plane]], this is equivalent to the [[Polsby–Popper test]].  Alternatively, the shape's area could be compared to that of its [[bounding circle]],<ref name="r1"/><ref name="r2"/> its [[convex hull]],<ref name="r1"/><ref name="r3"/> or its [[minimum bounding box]].<ref name="r3"/>

Similarly, a comparison can be made between the perimeter of the shape and that of its convex hull,<ref name="r3"/> its bounding circle,<ref name="r1"/> or a circle having the same area.<ref name="r1"/>

Other tests involve determining how much area overlaps with a circle of the same area<ref name="r2"/> or a reflection of the shape itself.<ref name="r1"/>

Compactness measures can be defined for three-dimensional shapes as well, typically as functions of [[volume]] and surface [[area]].  One example of a compactness measure is [[sphericity]] <math>\Psi</math>.  Another measure in use is <math>(\text{surface area})^{1.5}/(\text{volume})</math>,<ref>{{US patent|6169817}}</ref> which is proportional to <math>\Psi^{-3/2}</math>.

For [[Raster graphics|raster]] shapes, ''i.e.'' shapes composed of pixels or cells, some tests involve distinguishing between exterior and interior edges (or faces).<ref name="r2"/><ref name="r5"/>

More sophisticated measures of compactness include calculating the shape's [[moment of inertia]]<ref name="r2"/><ref name="r3"/> or boundary [[curvature]].<ref name="r3"/>

==Applications==
A common use of compactness measures is in [[redistricting]].  The goal is to maximize the compactness of [[constituency|electoral districts]], subject to other constraints, and thereby to avoid [[gerrymandering]].<ref>Rick Gillman "Geometry and Gerrymandering", Math Horizons, Vol. 10, #1 (Sep, 2002) 10-13.</ref>  Another use is in [[zoning]], to regulate the manner in which land can be subdivided into [[lot (real estate)|building lots]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Alec |last=MacGillis |title=Proposed Rule Aims to Tame Irregular Housing Lots
 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/11/14/AR2006111401154.html |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |page=B5 | date=2006-11-15 | access-date=2006-11-15 }}</ref>

==Human perception==
There is evidence that ''compactness'' is one of the basic dimensions of shape features extracted by the human visual system.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Huang|first=Liqiang|title=Space of preattentive shape features|journal=Journal of Vision|year=2020|language=en|volume=20|issue=4|pages=10|doi=10.1167/jov.20.4.10|pmid=32315405|pmc=7405702 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
